Indiana Casino Referendums Rejected in All Three Counties

Published November 5, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Voters in three northeastern Indiana counties soundly rejected ballot questions on Tuesday that would have cleared the way for a new commercial casino in the region. Allen County voters turned down the measure by roughly 60%, DeKalb County by about 65%, and Steuben County by nearly 60%, according to unofficial results reported by Casino.org. The outcome ends, at least for now, a push that had been building since state lawmakers opened the door to the idea earlier this year.

What the referendums would have allowed

The three county votes stemmed from House Bill 1038, signed into law in March by Governor Mike Braun, which let local voters decide whether to permit "inland casino gambling" — slots, table games, and sports betting — in their county. The legislation was tied to a long-running effort by Full House Resorts to relocate its Rising Star casino license away from Rising Sun, in the state's southeast corner, to a new site elsewhere in Indiana. Of the three counties on the ballot, Allen County — home to Fort Wayne — was widely viewed as the most commercially attractive landing spot, and a CBRE market study commissioned by the Indiana Gaming Commission had projected close to 1,000 permanent jobs and $28.1 million in annual local tax revenue if a casino were built there.

A one-sided campaign that still wasn't enough

Despite earlier reporting on a Fort Wayne-focused political action committee raising money ahead of the vote, Tuesday's result shows the pro-casino side was unable to overcome organized local opposition. The "Save Fort Wayne" campaign ran ads tying the proposal to addiction, divorce, bankruptcy, and poverty, and that message appears to have carried all three counties by comfortable margins. Full House Resorts CEO Daniel Lee, whose company's relocation plans depended on a county actually approving a site, said after the vote that the company's existing Rising Star property "makes money and we will continue to do that for our shareholders," signaling the casino's current location isn't going anywhere in the near term.

Indiana remains at 13 licensed commercial casinos following the vote. Whether Full House Resorts or another operator pursues a similar relocation effort in a different Indiana county in a future election cycle remains an open question.

Sources
